title: JavaScript Scope & Closures: Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Night-before revision notes on var/let/const, hoisting, the temporal dead zone, lexical scope, closures and their common uses, the loop closure pitfall, IIFEs and modules.

chapters.title: Variables and Scope Mental Model
points: var is function-scoped, let and const are block-scoped (a block is any { } such as if, for or a bare block)
const forbids reassigning the binding, not mutating the value: const a = []; a.push(1) works, a = [] throws TypeError
Lexical scope: a variable's visibility is fixed by where it is written in the source, not by where the function is called
Scope chain lookup: the engine checks the current scope, then each enclosing scope outward to global, and throws ReferenceError if not found
Only var at global level (and function declarations) attach to window/globalThis; let and const at global level do not

chapters.title: Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
points: Hoisting: declarations are registered at scope creation before code runs, so the name exists from the top of its scope
var is hoisted and initialised to undefined: console.log(x); var x = 5 prints undefined, not an error
let and const are hoisted but left uninitialised; access before the declaration line throws ReferenceError (the temporal dead zone, TDZ)
Function declarations hoist with their body so they can be called earlier; function expressions assigned to var hoist only as undefined, so calling early throws TypeError: not a function
typeof on a TDZ variable throws ReferenceError, unlike typeof on an undeclared name which returns 'undefined'

chapters.title: Closures: How They Work and Where to Use Them
points: A closure is a function bundled with a reference to the scope where it was created; it keeps that scope alive after the outer function returns
Closures capture variables by reference, not by value: if the outer variable changes later, the inner function sees the new value
Private state: function counter(){ let n = 0; return () => ++n } gives a counter whose n cannot be touched from outside
Function factories and partial application: function mul(a){ return b => a*b } then const double = mul(2)
Other common uses: callbacks and event handlers that remember data, memoisation caches, once/debounce wrappers

chapters.title: The Loop Closure Pitfall
points: Bug: for (var i=0;i<3;i++){ setTimeout(()=>console.log(i)) } prints 3 3 3 because all callbacks share one function-scoped i, which is 3 when they run
Fix 1: use let in the loop head; each iteration gets a fresh binding copy, so it prints 0 1 2
Fix 2 (legacy): wrap the body in an IIFE that takes i as a parameter: (function(j){ setTimeout(()=>console.log(j)) })(i)
Fix 3: use forEach or map whose callback parameter is a new scope per element
Same pitfall appears when attaching click handlers in a var loop; the handler reads the final index

chapters.title: IIFE and Modules
points: IIFE (immediately invoked function expression): (function(){ ... })(); creates a private scope and runs once, and the wrapping parentheses make it an expression
Module pattern: an IIFE returns an object of public methods while variables inside stay private through closures
ES modules (import/export) have their own module scope, so top-level variables are not global; they are strict mode by default and loaded once and cached
Exports are live bindings: importers see updated values of an exported let, but cannot assign to the import
Use IIFE for old script-tag code; use ES modules for new code, and prefer const by default, let when reassigning, never var

chapters.title: Scope and Closures Cheat Sheet
points: Declarations table: var = function scope, hoisted as undefined, redeclarable; let = block scope, TDZ, no redeclare; const = block scope, TDZ, no reassign
Default rule: const first, let if reassigned, avoid var
Hoisting rules: var undefined, let/const ReferenceError in TDZ, function declaration fully hoisted, function expression only as its variable
Closure rule: inner function keeps reference to outer variables; each call of the outer function creates a new independent scope
Loop fix rule: let in the loop head gives per-iteration binding; var needs an IIFE
